opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because my sense of ambition has shifted quite a bit.

When I started working on AI for health, the ambitious goal felt like showing that a model could pass a medical exam or match clinicians on some benchmark. That was a meaningful milestone at the time, because it wasn't obvious these systems could handle medical knowledge at all. But looking back, it was a fairly narrow definition of success. Exams measure recall and reasoning in a clean, multiple-choice setting, and real medicine is nothing like that.

Over time, the bar has moved from "can the model answer medical questions?" to "does this actually make people healthier?" That's a much harder and more interesting target. It means caring about messy, real-world conversations: someone at 2 a.m. worried about a symptom, a caregiver trying to make sense of a lab report, a clinician in a low-resource setting who doesn't have a specialist to call. It means asking whether the model knows when to escalate, when to ask a follow-up question, and when to say it's uncertain, not just whether its final answer is correct.

So ambition now looks less like topping a leaderboard and more like building evaluations that reflect how people actually use these tools, working closely with physicians to define what good behavior looks like, and taking seriously the responsibility that comes with a huge number of people already turning to these models for health information.

The other shift is scale. Once you realize how many people are using these systems for health questions, the most ambitious thing isn't a flashy demo. It's raising the floor of quality and safety for everyone, especially people who don't have easy access to good care. If we can do that well, I think it's one of the most direct ways AI can improve people's lives in the near term.

r001.rationale: It mentions health safety and responsibility, but does not frame health work as a setting for pursuing OpenAI’s broader safety and alignment work.

r002.rationale: It describes shifting evaluation goals, but does not present iterative deployment as a way to bring society along with high-stakes technology.

r003.rationale: It says the initial exam-focused goal now seems narrow, but does not establish that this was roughly two years earlier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, honestly. When I started, "ambitious" to me meant performance. Can the model pass the medical licensing exam? Can it match physicians on a benchmark? That was the frame coming out of the Med-PaLM era, and it made sense at the time because nobody knew whether these systems could even reason about medicine competently. Getting that first signal felt like the whole game.

Now I think that was actually a pretty modest definition of ambition, even though it felt huge. Benchmarks are a proxy. Once you clear them, you realize the thing you actually care about is whether somebody's health outcome is different because this technology exists. And that's a completely different problem. It's not about whether the model knows the right answer to a board question. It's about whether a person who's confused and scared at two in the morning gets something useful, whether a clinician who's drowning in documentation gets time back for the patient in front of them, whether someone with no access to a specialist gets a second opinion that's actually good.

So the bar has moved from "is it smart" to "does it help, at scale, safely." And that's harder in ways that aren't glamorous. It means thinking about how people actually use it, where it fails, who it fails for, how you build trust with clinicians who are rightly skeptical. It means caring about the long tail of real cases instead of the clean cases on an exam.

The other shift is that I used to think of ambition as being about the frontier, the hardest medical reasoning problems. I still care about that. But I've come to think the more ambitious thing might be the boring thing: making good health information and good health support available to hundreds of millions of people who currently don't have it. That's not a research paper. It's a deployment problem, a safety problem, a product problem. And I think if we actually pull it off, it matters more than any benchmark result we've ever published.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that my sense of ambition has shifted from what a model can do to what actually changes for a patient. You can set a very ambitious technical goal—have a system that can reason through difficult medical questions—and still have a lot of work left before that translates into better care.

So the question becomes: Can we help someone understand what’s happening to them? Can we help them figure out the right next step? Can we make it easier for a clinician to give that person the attention they need? And can we do that reliably, for people with very different circumstances?

That’s a much broader ambition than answering a question correctly. It means thinking about the whole experience, including where the model should acknowledge uncertainty and where a human needs to be involved. To me, the ambitious outcome is making good care more accessible while earning the trust that requires.

sol-6.1.text:
When I started, I thought the ambitious thing was to build a model that could answer really hard medical questions. And that’s still important, but I’ve come to see it as one part of a much bigger problem.

The ambition now is more about whether we can actually help people get better care. Can we help someone understand what’s happening to them, figure out the right next step, and navigate a system that can be incredibly confusing? Can we help clinicians spend more of their time on the parts of medicine where their judgment and relationship with the patient matter most?

That’s a much higher bar than giving a good answer to a question. You have to understand the context, recognize when you’re missing information, and know when to bring a human into the loop. So I think my sense of ambition has shifted from demonstrating medical capability to making that capability useful and trustworthy in people’s lives.
